cards.explanation: The answer is what her petition is. The king asks, "Queen Esther, what is your petition? It will be given to you." (Esther 7:2). He asked her something like this at her first banquet (Esther 5:6), and the text says he asks "once more." I think he's curious what could be so big that she needed two banquets to say it, friends.

The answer is her life and her people's lives. Esther says, "…grant me my life as my petition, and the lives of my people as my request." (Esther 7:3). Half a kingdom was on the table, and she asked for lives instead. Nobody at that table could miss what she was asking for.

The answer is True. Esther says, "If we had merely been sold as menservants and maidservants, I would have remained silent…" (Esther 7:4). She says it wouldn't justify burdening the king. What she's facing is "…destruction, death, and annihilation." which is a whole different size of problem, friends.
The answer is Haman. Esther says, "The adversary and enemy is this wicked man—Haman!" (Esther 7:6). No hint, no maybe. She names the man who dined at her banquet. That took some nerve, friends.
The word is terror. "…Haman stood in terror before the king and queen." (Esther 7:6). Esther had just named him as the enemy. I think his wine suddenly didn't taste so good, bakers.

The word is fury. "In his fury, the king arose from drinking his wine and went to the palace garden…" (Esther 7:7). The text gives us his fury and where he went. It doesn't tell us why he went out there. Esther had just named Haman as the enemy (Esther 7:6).

The answer is that Haman begs Queen Esther for his life. He "…stayed behind to beg Queen Esther for his life, for he realized that the king was planning a terrible fate for him." (Esther 7:7). The woman he was plotting against is now the one he's begging. I'd call that a rough turn, friends.

The answer is False. The king says, "Would he actually assault the queen while I am in the palace?" and "As soon as the words had left the king’s mouth, they covered Haman’s face." (Esther 7:8). The text shows Haman's face covered, not Haman speaking. I think that covering is a sign things were going badly for him.

The answer is Mordecai. Harbonah says the gallows was built "…for Mordecai, who gave the report that saved the king." (Esther 7:9). Mordecai is Esther's cousin (Esther 2:7), and Haman had the gallows built for him. Now that very gallows comes up in front of the king, friends.

The answer is True. Harbonah speaks up, and the king declares, "Hang him on it!" (Esther 7:9). The gallows was at Haman's house. The text says they hanged Haman on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai (Esther 7:10). The story isn't over, friends.
